topics.title: The basics of Dart
topics.summary: The language Flutter is written in: how it stops null crashes, the difference between final and const that everybody gets wrong, and what Dart 3 added.

lesson.heading: Null safety: the value that might not be there
lesson.body:
The commonest crash in most languages is using something that is not there. Dart removes it by splitting every type in two.

`String` means **there is always text in here**. `String?`, with a question mark, means **there might be text, or there might be nothing**. They are different types and the compiler will not let you mix them up.

Three pieces of syntax do nearly all the work:

**`?.`** — carry on only if there is something; otherwise the whole thing is null.
**`??`** — this, or if it is null, that.
**`??=`** — assign, but only if it is currently null.

And there is **promotion**, which is the pleasant part: once you have checked that something is not null, Dart remembers for the rest of that block and lets you use it as a normal value, with no `!` anywhere.

Promotion has one limit worth knowing, because the error message confuses people: it does not work on a **field of a class**, only on a local variable. The reason is that a field could be changed by something else between your check and your use. Copy it into a local first and it works.

lesson.heading: final and const are not the same thing
lesson.body:
This is the Dart question asked more than any other, and the answer is one sentence: **`final` is decided while the app runs, `const` is decided while it is compiled**.

`final` means "assigned once". The value can be worked out at the moment it is needed — the current time, something read from disk. You just cannot point the name at something else afterwards.

`const` means "known before the app ever runs". It has to be a value the compiler can work out on its own, so `DateTime.now()` can never be `const`.

Two consequences, and the second is why `const` matters so much in Flutter.

**Neither freezes the contents.** A `final` list can still have things added to it: what is frozen is the name, not the list. A `const` list genuinely cannot be changed, because it was built once and is shared.

**Two identical `const` values are literally the same object.** The compiler creates one and reuses it everywhere. That is the whole reason a `const` widget makes Flutter faster: it is the same instance as last time, so the framework can skip it entirely.

lesson.heading: late, and the three kinds of parameter
lesson.body:
**`late`** says "this will have a value before anyone reads it, but not yet". It is for something that cannot be set where it is declared — a controller built in `initState`, a value that depends on something else.

It buys you a non-nullable type without a `?` on every use. The price is that if somebody does read it first, you get a clear error at that moment rather than a vague null.

`late` with an initialiser is a different and useful thing: **the value is worked out the first time it is read**, not at startup. That is Dart's lazy property, and it is how you avoid paying for something expensive that may never be needed.

Parameters come in three kinds, and the names matter at the call site:

**Positional and required** — `f(int a)`. In order, no name.
**Named** — `f({int b = 0})`, written in braces. Given by name, in any order, and optional unless marked `required`.
**Positional and optional** — `f([int? b])`, in square brackets. Rare.

In Flutter nearly everything is named, and it is why a widget with twelve properties is still readable.

lesson.heading: Mixins and extensions
lesson.body:
Dart has single inheritance — one parent — but two other ways of sharing behaviour.

A **mixin** adds methods to a class without being its parent. A class can use as many as it likes, which is why they are so common in Flutter: `SingleTickerProviderStateMixin` is the one you meet first.

The word **`on`** limits where a mixin can be used: `mixin Logger on Widget` means only subtypes of `Widget` may use it. That is what lets the mixin call the methods of what it is mixed into, safely.

An **extension** adds a method to a type you do not own — including one from the standard library. You write `extension StringX on String` and from then on every string has your method.

The thing worth knowing, because it is asked: **extensions are chosen by the declared type, not the real one**. Call your extension through a variable declared as `Object`, and the one on `Object` is used, even if the value is really a `String`. Real methods behave the other way round. The reason is simple: an extension is not really added to the type; the compiler turns it into an ordinary function and decides which one while compiling.

lesson.heading: Dart 3: records, patterns and sealed
lesson.body:
Dart 3 added three things that change how everyday code is written.

**Records** are an anonymous group of values: `(3, 'a')`. For returning two things from a function without inventing a class for it. They compare by value, so two records with the same contents are equal — which is not what happens with ordinary classes.

**Patterns** let you take things apart and match their shape in one step. You can match a record, a list, an object's fields, and add a condition with `when`. It replaces a stack of `if`s with something you can read.

**`sealed`** means the subtypes are all known, because they must be in the same file. From that comes the thing that makes it worth using: a `switch` over a sealed type **does not need a default**, and the day somebody adds a subtype, every switch that does not handle it stops compiling. The compiler walks you to each place that needs updating.

The order of the cases matters and is the usual trap: the first match wins, so a specific case has to come before a general one, or the general one swallows it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `final` and `const`?
options: A const can be reassigned once
`final` is decided while running, `const` while compiling
questions.explanation: `final` is assigned once but the value can be worked out while the app runs — the current time, for instance. `const` has to be knowable before the app ever runs, which is also why two identical consts are literally the same object.
whyWrong: They are genuinely different, and in Flutter the difference affects performance.
Neither can be reassigned: that is what both of them mean.
Both work on fields, local variables and parameters alike.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `a` starts as null, so `b` takes the fallback 5. Then `??=` sets `a` to 10, because it was null. `b` was worked out before that and keeps its 5.
whyWrong: `a` is no longer null: the `??=` on the line before set it to 10.
`b` is 5: it was given its value while `a` was still null.
It compiles: these are the ordinary null operators.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Identical consts are built once by the compiler and reused, so `a` and `b` are literally the same object: true. `c` is `final`, built fresh while the app runs, so it is a different object: false. This sharing is exactly why `const` widgets make Flutter faster.
whyWrong: `a` and `b` are the same object: that is what `const` does.
`c` cannot be the same object: it is built separately at runtime.
It is the wrong way round on both.

questions.prompt: What happens here?
options: It fails at runtime with LateInitializationError
questions.explanation: `late` is a promise that the value will be there before anyone reads it. Reading it first breaks the promise, and Dart says so clearly with a dedicated error — which is far more useful than a vague null somewhere else.
whyWrong: Dart invents no default value: that would hide the mistake.
It cannot be null: the type is `int`, not `int?`. That is the point of `late`.
It compiles: the compiler cannot know whether something will set it in time.

questions.prompt: Given `void f(int a, {int b = 1, required int c})`, which call is valid?
questions.explanation: `a` is positional, so it is given in order with no name. `c` is named and required, so it must be given by name. `b` has a default and can be left out. Hence `f(1, c: 3)`.
whyWrong: `b` and `c` are named: they cannot be passed by position.
`a` is positional, so it must not have a name.
`c` is missing, and it is required.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Extensions are chosen while compiling, from the **declared** type. `s` is declared as `Object`, so the extension on `Object` is used, even though the value is really a `String`. Real methods behave the opposite way, which is why this surprises people.
whyWrong: `str` would need `s` to be declared as a `String`. The real type is not consulted.
There is no ambiguity: the declared type decides, and it is `Object`.
Nothing fails: a method is found, just not the one you expected.

questions.prompt: What does `sealed` guarantee in Dart 3?
options: It stops the subtypes being instantiated
It allows extension only from other packages
The subtypes are all known, so a switch can be checked
questions.explanation: Subtypes must be in the same library, so the compiler knows them all. A `switch` over a sealed type therefore needs no default — and the day somebody adds a subtype, every switch missing it stops compiling, which is exactly what you want.
whyWrong: The subtypes can be instantiated normally. It is the sealed class itself that cannot.
Immutability is a separate matter, decided by whether the fields are final.
It is the opposite: extension is limited to the same library.

questions.prompt: What does `print((1, 'a') == (1, 'a'));` print?
questions.explanation: Records compare by **value**: two records with the same contents in the same order are equal. That is different from ordinary classes, where without writing `==` yourself, two separate objects are never equal.
whyWrong: `false` is what you would get from two instances of a normal class with no `==` of its own.
Records have been part of the language since Dart 3.
`hashCode` is generated from the contents too, so it agrees with `==`.

questions.prompt: What does `on` mean in `mixin Logger on Widget`?
options: It can be used on any class
It can only be used on subtypes of Widget
It overrides all of Widget's methods
questions.explanation: `on` sets the requirement for using the mixin, and that is what lets the mixin safely call `Widget`'s own methods — it knows whatever uses it will have them.
whyWrong: A mixin does not extend anything: it is added to a class, not placed above it.
Without `on` it would be usable anywhere. The whole purpose of `on` is to restrict it.
It overrides nothing: it adds, and only replaces what it explicitly declares.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The cases are tried from the top. `(0, 0)` does not match because the first value is 3. The second matches the shape and its `when` holds, since 3 is above 0 — so it wins and nothing below is tried. Order matters: move that case lower and the general one would swallow it.
whyWrong: `origin` needs both values to be 0, and the first is 3.
The more specific case came first and matched, so this one is never reached.
The catch-all is only used when nothing above matches.

topics.title: Widgets and the life of a screen
topics.summary: Everything on screen is a widget; what the difference between stateless and stateful really is, when each method runs, and why `const` matters more than it looks.

lesson.heading: Everything is a widget, and widgets are thrown away
lesson.body:
In Flutter every single thing is a **widget**: a button, a piece of text, padding, even the alignment of something. You do not change widgets — you build new ones.

That is the idea to get right first, because it explains everything else. A widget is not the thing on screen. It is a **description** of what the screen should look like, and it is immutable: once built, it never changes. When something changes, Flutter builds a **new** widget and works out the difference.

Under the description there are two more trees, and this is what the questions are really about:

**The widget tree** — your descriptions. Cheap, created and thrown away constantly.
**The element tree** — the long-lived objects that hold position in the tree and keep the state. These survive rebuilds.
**The render tree** — the things that actually measure and paint.

So rebuilding does not mean redrawing everything. Flutter compares the new description with the old, keeps the elements where the type and key match, and only touches what genuinely differs. That is why building widgets in a `build` method is cheap, and why you are expected to do it on every frame.

lesson.heading: Stateless and stateful
lesson.body:
**`StatelessWidget`** describes something that depends only on what it was given. Same inputs, same output. Use it whenever you can — which is more often than people think.

**`StatefulWidget`** is for something that has to remember between builds: a counter, whether a panel is open, an animation's progress, a text field's controller.

The part that confuses everybody at first is that a `StatefulWidget` is **two classes**. The widget itself is still immutable and still thrown away on every rebuild. The `State` object is the one that survives, and it is where your variables live.

That separation is the whole point: the parent can rebuild and hand down a new widget as often as it likes, and the state is not lost, because the state does not live in the widget.

**`setState`** does one thing: it marks the element as needing a rebuild and asks the framework to do it before the next frame. It does not rebuild immediately, and it does not rebuild the whole app. Changing a variable without it is the classic bug — the value really does change, and the screen simply never finds out.

lesson.heading: When each method runs
lesson.body:
A `State` has a handful of methods, and knowing which runs when is the most-asked thing in this topic.

**`initState`** — once, when the state is created. Set up controllers, subscribe to a stream. You cannot use `InheritedWidget`s here — more on that below.
**`didChangeDependencies`** — right after `initState`, and again whenever something it depends on changes. This is where `Theme.of(context)` is safe.
**`build`** — every time something needs redrawing. Can run many times a second. Keep it cheap and free of side effects.
**`didUpdateWidget`** — when the parent rebuilds and hands down a new widget with different values. Use it to react: if the id changed, reload.
**`deactivate`** — removed from the tree, possibly to be reinserted elsewhere.
**`dispose`** — gone for good. **Release everything here**: controllers, subscriptions, timers.

The pairing is the thing to remember: **whatever you create in `initState` you release in `dispose`**. A forgotten `dispose` is the most common leak in Flutter, and it shows up as an app that gets slower the longer it is used.

And the reason `Theme.of(context)` fails in `initState`: that call registers a dependency, so the widget is rebuilt when the theme changes. In `initState` the element is not yet in a position to register one. `didChangeDependencies` is.

lesson.heading: BuildContext: where you are in the tree
lesson.body:
A **`BuildContext`** is not a global thing and it is not a bag of utilities. It is **your widget's element**: its position in the tree. That is why every `build` receives one, and why they are all different.

That is also the whole explanation for `Theme.of(context)` and `Navigator.of(context)`. `of` means "climb up from here until you find one". Using the wrong context means climbing from the wrong place, which is why a `Scaffold.of(context)` called with the context of the widget that built the Scaffold fails: from there, there is no Scaffold above.

The second thing is the one that bites in real apps: **using a context after an `await`**. During the wait, the user may have closed the screen, and the context now points at an element that is no longer in the tree. The result is a crash or something silently wrong.

The fix is one line: check `context.mounted` after every `await` before touching the context. The linter warns you about this, and it is worth leaving that warning switched on.

lesson.heading: const: the cheapest optimisation there is
lesson.body:
When a parent rebuilds, Flutter walks its children and compares each new widget with the old one. If it can tell nothing has changed, it skips the whole subtree.

A **`const` widget** makes that comparison trivial. Because identical consts are built once by the compiler and shared, the new widget **is literally the same object** as the old one. The comparison is a pointer check, it passes, and everything below is skipped.

Without `const`, a new object is created on every build, the comparison fails, and the subtree is visited again — even though it draws exactly the same thing.

The habit worth building: **put `const` on anything that does not depend on a variable**. Separators, icons, fixed text, padding. The linter can tell you where it is possible, and it costs nothing to accept.

A practical trick that follows: if part of a widget is expensive and does not change, pulling it into a `const` child — or holding it in a field — stops it being rebuilt with the rest. That is often a bigger win than anything clever.

questions.prompt: Where do you create an `AnimationController` in a stateful widget?
questions.explanation: `initState` runs once, which is what you want for something that must exist for the life of the screen. And whatever you create there you release in `dispose`, or the controller keeps ticking after the screen has gone.
whyWrong: `build` can run many times a second: you would create a new controller on every frame.
The widget is thrown away on every rebuild. State belongs in the `State`, not the widget.
`didUpdateWidget` only runs when the parent hands down something new, which may never happen.

questions.prompt: What does `setState` do?
options: Marks the element as needing a rebuild, before the next frame
questions.explanation: It does not rebuild straight away: it notes that this element is out of date and the framework rebuilds it before the next frame. That is why several `setState` calls in a row cost one rebuild, not several.
whyWrong: Neither immediately nor the whole tree: only this element and what it builds.
Nothing is saved anywhere. It is purely about redrawing.
The `State` survives: recreating it would lose everything, which is the opposite of the point.

questions.prompt: Why is `Theme.of(context)` a problem in `initState`?
options: The Theme does not exist before the first frame
You cannot register a dependency there: use didChangeDependencies
questions.explanation: `Theme.of` does two things: it finds the theme, and it records that this widget depends on it, so it is rebuilt when the theme changes. In `initState` the element is not yet able to register that, so it throws. `didChangeDependencies` runs immediately afterwards and is the right place.
whyWrong: The theme exists: the problem is the registration, not the value.
The context is perfectly valid in `initState`. It just cannot be used for this.
It is not allowed at all: it fails, it is not slow.

questions.prompt: The parent rebuilds and hands down a new `title`. What runs before `build`?
questions.explanation: The state survives, so `initState` is not called again. `didUpdateWidget` is called instead, with the old widget as its argument, so you can compare and react — reloading if an id changed, for instance.
whyWrong: `initState` runs once, when the state is created. The state here already exists.
That runs when an inherited widget this depends on changes, which is a different event.
`createState` runs once, right at the start.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
options: Navigator cannot be used in onPressed
setState is missing after the await
It uses the context after an await, with no check
const is not allowed on Text
questions.explanation: During the `await` the user may have left the screen. The context would then point at an element no longer in the tree, and using it crashes or misbehaves. The fix is `if (!context.mounted) return;` straight after the await.
whyWrong: It can: that is the normal place for it.
Nothing here needs a rebuild: the screen is being closed.
`const Text('Save')` is correct and is exactly what you should write.

questions.prompt: When is a `StatelessWidget` the right choice?
options: When it depends only on its parameters and on inherited widgets
questions.explanation: If everything it draws comes from what it was given, there is nothing to remember and nothing to keep between builds. Stateless widgets are simpler, cheaper and easier to test — reach for stateful only when something genuinely has to survive a rebuild.
whyWrong: It can have as many children as you like: that has nothing to do with it.
Network calls belong somewhere else entirely, not inside a widget's build.
It is the most common kind of widget there is.

questions.prompt: Why does a `const` widget save work when the parent rebuilds?
options: It is literally the same instance, so Flutter skips the subtree
It is painted on its own layer
It is compiled to native code
questions.explanation: Identical consts are built once by the compiler and shared, so the new widget is the same object as the old one. The comparison is a pointer check, it passes, and everything below is skipped — no rebuild, no comparison, nothing.
whyWrong: Layers are about painting and have nothing to do with `const`.
It has an element like any other widget. What changes is that the comparison succeeds instantly.
`const` is about when the value is created, not about how it is compiled.

questions.prompt: What exactly is a `BuildContext`?
options: The widget's element, its position in the tree
questions.explanation: It is the element: where this widget sits in the tree. That is why `Theme.of(context)` works by climbing upwards from there, and why using the context of the wrong widget looks in the wrong place.
whyWrong: There is nothing global about it: every widget has its own, and they differ.
The render object is what measures and paints. The context sits above that.
It has nothing to do with the State: stateless widgets have a context too.

questions.prompt: What is missing from this State?
questions.explanation: The subscription is created in `initState` and never cancelled, so it carries on after the screen is gone — calling `setState` on a state that no longer exists. Whatever you create in `initState` you release in `dispose`. It is the most common leak in Flutter.
whyWrong: `super.build()` is only needed with certain mixins, and it has nothing to do with the leak.
`setState` in `initState` would be pointless: a build is already coming.
Making it nullable changes nothing: it would still never be cancelled.

questions.prompt: A widget is inserted and then permanently removed. What is the right order?
options: createState, initState, didChangeDependencies, build, deactivate, dispose
questions.explanation: The state is created, set up, told about its dependencies, built, then taken out of the tree (`deactivate`) and finally destroyed (`dispose`). `deactivate` comes first because a widget can be removed and reinserted elsewhere; only when that does not happen does `dispose` follow.
whyWrong: `dispose` is always last: `deactivate` comes before it.
`build` cannot come before `initState`: nothing would be set up yet.
`didUpdateWidget` only happens if the parent hands down a new widget, which is not part of a simple insert and remove.

topics.title: Layout: how sizes are decided
topics.summary: One rule explains almost every layout problem in Flutter — and once you have it, the yellow-and-black stripes stop being a mystery.

lesson.heading: The one rule
lesson.body:
Flutter decides sizes in three steps, and almost every layout question is really about this one sentence:

**Constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent decides the position.**

In detail: a parent tells each child what sizes are allowed — a minimum and a maximum width and height. The child picks a size **within those limits** and reports it back. The parent then decides where to put it.

Three consequences follow, and they explain the most common surprises:

**A widget cannot choose its position.** It only reports a size; where it goes is its parent's decision. So "why is my widget not in the middle?" is always a question about the parent.

**A constraint can be tight** — minimum equals maximum — in which case the child has no choice at all. That is why a `Container(width: 100)` placed directly at the root fills the whole screen: the root gives tight constraints the size of the screen, and the container has no say.

**Some widgets loosen constraints and some pass them on.** `Center`, `Align` and `Padding` loosen them, which is why wrapping that container in a `Center` suddenly makes it 100 by 100.

When a layout does something you did not expect, the question to ask is never "what is wrong with this widget?" but **"what constraints is its parent giving it?"**

lesson.heading: Row, Column and Expanded
lesson.body:
`Row` lays children out side by side, `Column` one above the other. They behave identically; only the direction differs.

Each has a **main axis** — horizontal for a `Row`, vertical for a `Column` — and a **cross axis**, the other one. `mainAxisAlignment` spreads the children along the main axis; `crossAxisAlignment` lines them up across it. Mixing those two up is the most common small confusion in Flutter layout.

The children are laid out in order and each gets as much as it asks for, until the space runs out — and then you get the overflow stripes.

**`Expanded`** is the answer to "take whatever is left". It gives its child tight constraints filling the remaining space, after the fixed-size children have had theirs. With several, `flex` shares the space in proportion.

**`Flexible`** is the gentler version: the child **may** use up to the available space but does not have to, so it can stay smaller. `Expanded` is exactly `Flexible` with a tight fit.

The practical rule: a `Text` that might be long, inside a `Row`, goes in an `Expanded`. That one habit removes most overflow errors before they happen.

lesson.heading: Overflow, and the unbounded error
lesson.body:
Two errors come up constantly, and they look similar but have opposite causes.

**The yellow-and-black stripes** mean the children asked for more space than there was. Something must either shrink or scroll. Usually the answer is wrapping a `Text` in `Expanded`, or the whole thing in a `SingleChildScrollView`.

**"viewport was given unbounded height"** is the opposite: a scrollable child was given **no limit at all** on how tall it could be. A `ListView` inside a `Column` is the classic case. The column says "be as tall as you like", the list says "I need to know how tall I can be before I can decide what to show", and neither can proceed.

The fix depends on what you want:

**`Expanded`** — the list takes the space left after the other children. This is almost always the right answer.
**`SizedBox(height: 200)`** — a fixed height, when you want one.
**`shrinkWrap: true`** — the list measures itself by laying out **every** child. It works, and with a long list it is slow, because it defeats the whole point of a lazy list. Only for a short list you know is short.

The habit worth having: a `ListView` inside a `Column` almost always wants an `Expanded` around it.

lesson.heading: Stack, LayoutBuilder and MediaQuery
lesson.body:
**`Stack`** puts children on top of one another, in the order given — the last one is on top. By itself it sizes to its largest child.

Inside it, **`Positioned`** pins a child to one or more edges: `Positioned(bottom: 16, right: 16, ...)` places something in the bottom-right corner with a margin. Children that are not positioned are aligned according to the stack's `alignment`.

For adapting to size, there are two tools, and choosing between them is a real question:

**`MediaQuery`** gives you facts about the **screen**: its size, the safe area, the text scale, whether dark mode is on. Use it for things that genuinely depend on the device.

**`LayoutBuilder`** gives you the constraints **this widget** has been given. Use it for anything that should adapt to the space it actually has — because a widget might be in a side panel, in a dialog, or in a split view, where the screen size tells you nothing useful.

The rule: **`LayoutBuilder` for layout, `MediaQuery` for the device.** A widget that decides its layout from the screen size breaks the moment somebody puts it in a smaller container.

lesson.heading: Lists and slivers
lesson.body:
**`ListView.builder`** only builds the items that are visible, plus a few just off screen. That is what lets a list of ten thousand rows exist at all. Using the plain `ListView(children: [...])` builds every one up front, so it is only for short lists.

When you need more than a plain list in one scroll — a header that collapses, then a list, then a grid, all scrolling together — you need **slivers**.

A sliver is a piece of a scrolling area that knows how to build only the part of itself that is visible. **`CustomScrollView`** holds several of them and scrolls them as one.

The common ones: `SliverAppBar` for a header that collapses or stays pinned, `SliverList` and `SliverGrid` for the content, `SliverToBoxAdapter` for fitting an ordinary widget in among them.

The mistake to avoid is nesting one scrollable inside another with `shrinkWrap`. It works, it looks right, and it builds every item of the inner list immediately — which is exactly what the lazy list was there to prevent. Slivers are the proper answer.

questions.prompt: What is the basic layout rule in Flutter?
options: The child chooses its own position and size
The parent always forces the exact size
Constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent positions
Layout is worked out while compiling
questions.explanation: The parent says what sizes are allowed, the child picks one within those limits and reports it, and the parent then decides where to put it. Almost every layout surprise is explained by looking at what constraints the parent is giving.
whyWrong: A child never chooses its position: that is always the parent's decision.
Only with tight constraints. Many widgets, like `Center`, deliberately loosen them.
It is worked out while the app runs, which is how it adapts to any screen.

questions.prompt: What happens with this layout?
options: An error: the viewport is given unbounded height
The list takes the remaining space
The list is visible but does not scroll
questions.explanation: A `Column` gives its children no height limit, and a `ListView` needs one to know how much to show. Neither can proceed, so Flutter reports it. The fix is `Expanded` around the list, which gives it exactly the space left over.
whyWrong: That is what `Expanded` would do. Without it, nothing tells the list how much space it has.
Overflow is a different error: that is asking for more space than there is, not for an unlimited amount.
There is nothing on screen to scroll: the error happens during layout.

questions.prompt: How do you make a child of a Row take all the remaining space?
questions.explanation: `Expanded` tells the row to give this child everything left after the fixed-size children have taken theirs. It is also the usual way to stop a long text overflowing.
whyWrong: `SizedBox.expand` fills its own constraints, which does not tell the row to share the space.
That changes how much space the row itself takes, not how it divides it among its children.
An infinite width inside a row is unbounded and produces an error.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `Expanded` and `Flexible`?
options: Expanded only works in a Column
Expanded is Flexible with a tight fit
Flexible forces the child to fill the space
questions.explanation: `Flexible` says the child **may** use up to that much space; `Expanded` says it **must** fill it. So `Expanded` is literally `Flexible(fit: FlexFit.tight)`. Use `Flexible` when the child should be allowed to stay smaller.
whyWrong: Both work in a Row and a Column alike.
Both use `flex` to share the space in proportion.
It is the other way round: `Flexible` allows, `Expanded` forces.

questions.prompt: What size is the container here?
options: The whole screen: the constraints are tight
questions.explanation: The root gives tight constraints the size of the screen — minimum equal to maximum — so the container has no choice and the 100s are ignored. Wrap it in a `Center` and the constraints are loosened, and then it really is 100 by 100.
whyWrong: For it to be 100x100 the constraints would have to be loose, and at the root they are not.
Nothing centres it: the root gives no such instruction.
`MaterialApp` is not required: `runApp` takes any widget.

questions.prompt: When should you use `LayoutBuilder` rather than `MediaQuery`?
options: To adapt to the space this widget has actually been given
questions.explanation: `MediaQuery` tells you about the screen; `LayoutBuilder` tells you about the box this widget is in. A widget that decides its layout from the screen size breaks the moment somebody puts it in a side panel or a dialog.
whyWrong: They answer different questions: neither is always better.
Pixel density is a property of the device, so that is `MediaQuery`.
The safe area is also a device fact, and also `MediaQuery`.

questions.prompt: A Row with a long text shows the overflow stripes. What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Wrap the text in Expanded or Flexible
Replace the Row with a Stack
questions.explanation: The text is asking for all the width it needs. `Expanded` gives it the space that is actually left, and with `overflow: TextOverflow.ellipsis` it ends in three dots instead of overflowing.
whyWrong: A smaller font hides the problem for one string and brings it back for a longer one.
A `Stack` overlaps children: it does not solve a width problem in a row.
That changes how much space the row takes, not how it shares it out.

questions.prompt: Why is `ListView(shrinkWrap: true)` with thousands of items a bad idea?
options: It has to lay out every child in order to measure itself
questions.explanation: To report its own height, the list has to know the height of everything in it — so it builds every item, immediately. That throws away the whole benefit of a lazy list. For a long list, `Expanded` or a sliver is the right answer.
whyWrong: Scrolling still works. The problem is the cost of measuring.
It is not deprecated: it is right for a short list whose length you know.
It concerns height, not width.

questions.prompt: You want a collapsing header, then a list, then a grid, all in one scroll. What do you use?
options: A Column with a ListView and a GridView
A CustomScrollView with SliverAppBar, SliverList and SliverGrid
questions.explanation: Slivers are made for exactly this: several pieces that scroll as one, each building only what is visible. A `CustomScrollView` holds them, and `SliverAppBar` gives you the collapsing header for free.
whyWrong: That nests scrollables inside a column, which gives the unbounded error or forces `shrinkWrap`.
`NestedScrollView` is for coordinating two separate scroll areas, such as tabs. It is not needed here.
`shrinkWrap` would build everything at once, which is what you are trying to avoid.

questions.prompt: In a Stack, how do you place a child 16 pixels from the bottom and the right?
options: Align with bottomRight and a margin
questions.explanation: `Positioned` is the widget made for this and only works inside a `Stack`. You give it the distances from the edges you care about and leave out the ones you do not.
whyWrong: Padding adds space around a child; it does not pin it to the edges of the stack.
`Transform.translate` moves something visually without changing where the layout thinks it is, which causes trouble with taps.
`Align` works, but it is less direct and more awkward to get exact distances from.

topics.title: Asynchronous Dart
topics.summary: Dart runs on one thread, so nothing may block it. Futures, streams, the two queues that decide the order of everything, and isolates for the heavy work.

lesson.heading: Future and async/await
lesson.body:
A **`Future`** is a promise of a value that is not here yet: the reply to a network call, a file being read. It has three states — waiting, done with a value, done with an error.

You could handle it with `.then()` and `.catchError()`, and with three steps that becomes unreadable. **`async`/`await`** says the same thing in a straight line: mark the function `async`, write `await` where you need the value, and the code below carries on after it has arrived.

Two things to be clear about, because both get asked:

**An `async` function always returns a `Future`.** Write `return 42` inside one and the type is `Future<int>`, not `int`. It cannot be otherwise: the caller may have to wait.

**`await` does not block the thread.** The function is suspended and the thread goes off to do other things — draw a frame, handle a tap. That is what keeps the interface alive while something slow happens.

Errors behave as you would hope: inside an `async` function you use `try`/`catch` exactly as in normal code. The catch is that you have to **actually await** the thing. Calling an `async` function without `await` starts it and carries on, so the error pops out somewhere else entirely, long after your `try` has finished.

lesson.heading: The event loop: two queues
lesson.body:
Dart runs your code on **one thread**. There is no parallelism inside an isolate — what there is, is a loop that takes one thing at a time from a queue and runs it to the end.

The part that explains all the surprising output orders is that there are **two** queues, and one always wins.

**The microtask queue** — small internal jobs, including everything that continues after an `await`.
**The event queue** — everything else: timers, taps, I/O, anything created with `Future(...)`.

The rule: **the microtask queue is emptied completely before a single event is taken from the event queue.** Not one microtask — all of them, including any added while it is draining.

From that comes the standard interview question. Normal code runs first, right through to the end of the current function. Then all the microtasks. Then one event. That is why `scheduleMicrotask` and `Future.microtask` always come before a plain `Future(...)`, whatever order you wrote them in.

And the practical consequence of there being one thread: **a long calculation blocks everything**. No await helps, because nothing is waiting — it is working. That is what isolates are for.

lesson.heading: Streams: many values over time
lesson.body:
A `Future` gives one value. A **`Stream`** gives a sequence of them over time: what a user types, the position from a sensor, messages from a socket.

You make one with `async*` and `yield`, and you read it with `await for` or `.listen()`. The same operators as a list are available — `map`, `where`, `reduce` — plus ones that only make sense over time.

The distinction that matters, and gets asked:

**Single-subscription** — the default. It can be listened to **once**. Listening twice throws. It is for a sequence of things that belong to one consumer: reading a file, a single HTTP response.

**Broadcast** — many listeners at once, and each only sees what arrives **after** it joined. For events several parts of the app care about.

The rule for the common bug: if you get a `StateError` about a stream already being listened to, you have a single-subscription stream and two listeners. Either call `.asBroadcastStream()`, or restructure so there is only one.

And like everything that subscribes, a subscription has to be **cancelled** — in `dispose`, when the screen goes. Otherwise it carries on, holding the state alive.

lesson.heading: Isolates: real parallelism
lesson.body:
`await` solves waiting. It does nothing for **working**: parsing ten megabytes of JSON takes a second of pure calculation, and during that second the thread cannot draw anything. The result is a visible freeze.

An **isolate** is a separate line of execution with its **own memory**. That is the key difference from a thread: isolates share nothing at all, so there are no locks and no races — the two bugs that make concurrent code hard in other languages simply cannot happen.

The price is that communication happens by **copying messages**, over ports. You cannot hand an object across; you send a copy. For large amounts of data that copy is itself a cost worth knowing about.

In practice you rarely create one by hand. **`Isolate.run`** does the whole thing in one line: it starts one, runs your function, hands back the result and shuts it down. (`compute` is the older Flutter equivalent.)

The rule for when: use an isolate when the work is **calculation** lasting more than a few milliseconds — parsing a lot of JSON, image processing, encryption. Do not use one for network or disk work, which is waiting, not working, and is already handled by `await`.

lesson.heading: Waiting for several things
lesson.body:
Three network calls one after another, each `await`ed, take the sum of their times. If they do not depend on each other, that is time thrown away.

**`Future.wait`** starts them all and waits for all of them. Three calls of one second each take one second in total. The results come back as a list, in the order you asked for them, however they actually finished.

The detail worth knowing: if one fails, `Future.wait` throws straight away — but the others are **not** cancelled, they carry on in the background. If you want every outcome, failures included, pass `eagerError: false` and catch each one, or wrap each future so it cannot throw.

**`Future.any`** gives you the first to finish, for when you have two sources and want whichever answers first.

And in Dart 3 there is a neater form for a fixed set: put the futures in a record and use `.wait`. You get a record back, with each value keeping its own type, instead of a list of a common supertype you then have to cast.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Normal code runs first, right to the end of `main`: A and E. Then the microtask queue is emptied completely, in the order the microtasks were added: C then D. Only then is an event taken from the event queue: B.
whyWrong: B and C cannot run before E: nothing scheduled interrupts code that is already running.
B is an event and the microtasks always go first, whatever order they were written in.
E is normal code and runs before anything that was scheduled.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: An `async` function runs normally until the first `await`: so A, then B. At the `await` it suspends and control returns to `main`, which prints C. Only afterwards does the continuation run, printing D.
whyWrong: B comes before C: `f()` really does run, as far as the first await.
A is first: it is printed before `f()` is even called.
D cannot come before C: at the await, control goes back to `main`.

questions.prompt: An `async` function whose body is `return 42;` has what return type?
questions.explanation: Marking a function `async` means it may suspend, so the caller may have to wait. The value is therefore always wrapped in a `Future`, even when nothing is actually awaited inside.
whyWrong: A plain `int` would mean the value is available immediately, and `async` is exactly the promise that it might not be.
A `Stream` is for several values over time. A function returns one.
`FutureOr` is a type you can write in a signature, but an `async` function always produces a `Future`.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call `listen` twice on a single-subscription stream?
options: The second listener only gets new events
questions.explanation: A single-subscription stream is designed for exactly one consumer — reading a file, one HTTP response — so a second listener is an error, not a silent surprise. If you need several, call `.asBroadcastStream()`.
whyWrong: That is what a broadcast stream does. This one refuses outright.
It is not built to send the same values to two places.
Nothing is cancelled: the second call simply fails.

questions.prompt: Why parse a 10 MB JSON with `Isolate.run`?
options: To avoid blocking the thread that draws the interface
So that the result can be awaited
questions.explanation: Parsing is pure calculation, and Dart runs on one thread. A second of calculation is a second with no frames drawn, which the user sees as a freeze. An isolate does the work elsewhere and sends the result back.
whyWrong: `jsonDecode` is synchronous, which is precisely the problem: it runs to the end without yielding.
Isolates share nothing at all. That is what makes them safe and why they communicate by copying.
You can await a `Future` without an isolate. Awaiting is not the point.

questions.prompt: How do two isolates communicate?
questions.explanation: Each isolate has its own memory, so nothing is shared and messages are copies sent over `SendPort` and `ReceivePort`. That is why races and deadlocks cannot happen — and why sending a very large object has a cost of its own.
whyWrong: A static variable in one isolate is invisible to the other: each has its own copy.
There is nothing to lock, because nothing is shared.
The heaps are separate: that is the whole design.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `reduce` combines the values as they arrive, two at a time: 1+2 is 3, then 3+3 is 6. It gives back a single `Future` with the final result, which is why it is awaited.
whyWrong: 3 is the number of values, not their total.
A list is what `toList()` would give. `reduce` collapses them into one value.
That is what you would print without the `await`.

questions.prompt: What happens here?
options: An unhandled error: the await is missing
questions.explanation: Without `await`, `fail()` is started and `main` carries on. The error appears later, inside the future, with nothing attached to catch it — so it surfaces as an unhandled error. The `try` finished long before. The fix is `await fail();`.
whyWrong: The `try` has already finished by the time the error happens.
There is definitely an error: it is just reported where you were not looking.
It compiles: the linter warns about the unawaited future, but it is valid Dart.

questions.prompt: Three independent network calls. How do you run them together and wait for all?
questions.explanation: `Future.wait` starts all three at once and finishes when the last one does, so three one-second calls take one second instead of three. The results come back in the order you asked for them.
whyWrong: Three awaits in a row run them one after another: the times add up.
`Future.any` gives you the first to answer and ignores the rest. That is a different question.
Isolates are for calculation. Network calls are waiting, and `await` already handles that.

questions.prompt: When is the microtask queue emptied?
options: Completely, before each event is taken from the event queue
After timers but not after I/O
Only when the event queue is empty
questions.explanation: The loop empties the microtask queue entirely — including microtasks added while it is draining — and only then takes one event. That is why a continuation after an `await` always runs before a plain `Future(...)`, and also why an endless microtask loop freezes the app completely.
whyWrong: It has nothing to do with frames: it happens between events, as often as needed.
It applies between every event, of whatever kind.
It is the other way round: the microtasks are emptied first, then one event is taken.

topics.title: Trees and Keys
topics.summary: The Widget, Element, and RenderObject trees, reconciliation, Keys, and InheritedWidget

lesson.heading: The three trees
lesson.body:
The **Widget tree** holds cheap, immutable configurations that are recreated on every build. The **Element tree** holds the live instances: it manages the lifecycle, holds the `State`, and connects widgets to render objects. The **RenderObject tree** handles layout, paint, and hit testing.

Elements and RenderObjects are expensive and get **reused** as much as possible: a rebuild creates new widgets, but usually just updates the existing objects.

lesson.heading: Rebuilds and reconciliation
lesson.body:
When a parent rebuilds, Flutter calls `Widget.canUpdate(old, new)` for each child: if `runtimeType` and `key` match, the existing Element is **updated** with the new widget and the State is preserved. Otherwise the Element is unmounted and a new one is created, losing its state.

For lists of children, the comparison happens by position unless there are keys: in that case Flutter matches children by key.

lesson.heading: Local keys
lesson.body:
Keys matter when stateful **sibling children of the same type** are reordered, inserted, or removed. Without keys, the State stays tied to the position and "slides" onto the wrong item.

`ValueKey` compares a value with `==` (typically an id), `ObjectKey` compares object identity, and `UniqueKey` is different from every other key and always forces a new Element. The key goes on the **root widget of each item**, at the sibling level.

lesson.heading: GlobalKey
lesson.body:
A `GlobalKey` is unique across the entire app: it gives you access to a widget's `currentState` or `currentContext` (e.g. `FormState.validate()`) and lets you move a subtree to a different position **while keeping its state**.

It's more expensive than local keys and should be created **only once** (in a State field), never inside `build`: a new GlobalKey on every build recreates the subtree and loses its state.

lesson.heading: InheritedWidget
lesson.body:
An `InheritedWidget` makes data available to its entire subtree. A descendant that calls `dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType` gets the data in O(1) and **registers itself as a dependent**: it will be rebuilt when the widget changes and `updateShouldNotify` returns true.

`getInheritedWidgetOfExactType` reads without registering a dependency. `Theme.of`, `MediaQuery.of`, and Provider are all built on this mechanism.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Typical question: **"When do you need keys?"** Concise answer: when a collection of stateful widgets of the same type changes order or composition; without keys Flutter matches by position and the State ends up on the wrong item. Mention `canUpdate` (runtimeType + key).

If they ask about the three trees, explain that widgets are cheap blueprints, Elements are the bridge that preserves state, and RenderObjects do layout and paint: that's what keeps frequent rebuilds cheap.

questions.prompt: Which tree handles layout and paint?
questions.explanation: RenderObjects compute size, position, and painting. Widgets are just configuration, and Elements manage the lifecycle.
whyWrong: Widgets are just immutable descriptions of the UI: they don't compute sizes or paint anything.
Elements manage the lifecycle and the link between widgets and RenderObjects, but layout and paint belong to RenderObjects.
The Semantics tree is for accessibility (screen readers), not for layout or painting.

questions.prompt: When does Flutter reuse an existing Element with the new widget?
options: Always, if they're in the same position
When they have the same children
questions.explanation: That's the `Widget.canUpdate` rule. If the type or key changes, the Element is unmounted and recreated, and the State is lost.
whyWrong: Flutter doesn't use `==` to decide on reuse; it uses `Widget.canUpdate`, which compares `runtimeType` and `key`.
Position isn't enough: if the type or key changes, the Element is unmounted and recreated even in the same spot.
Children aren't part of `canUpdate`: they're reconciled afterwards, one by one.

questions.prompt: A list of Stateful tiles with checkboxes: you remove the first one and the "checked" state lands on the wrong tile. The fix?
options: A single GlobalKey for the list
questions.explanation: Without keys, Elements are matched by position. With a stable key tied to the id, each State follows its own item.
whyWrong: A GlobalKey identifies a single widget, not the items in a list: it doesn't fix how sibling tiles are matched.
Calling `setState` multiple times doesn't change how Elements are matched by position: you need a stable key.
`const` avoids unnecessary rebuilds but doesn't give the tiles an identity: without keys, the States stay tied to position.

questions.prompt: What happens on every rebuild with this code?
options: A new key: the TextField loses its text and focus
questions.explanation: Every build creates a different GlobalKey, so `canUpdate` fails: the Element is recreated with a new State. GlobalKeys should be created only once.
whyWrong: `GlobalKey()` creates a new object on every `build` call: the previous key isn't reused.
There's no duplicate, because only one GlobalKey exists in the tree at any moment; the problem is that it changes on every build.
With a different key `canUpdate` fails: the Element and State are recreated, not just repainted.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `ValueKey` and `ObjectKey`?
options: ValueKey is global, ObjectKey is local
questions.explanation: Both are LocalKeys. ValueKey compares the value with `==`; ObjectKey compares object identity, which is useful when there's no unique id.
whyWrong: Both are LocalKeys, compared among siblings; the global keys are GlobalKeys.
ObjectKey accepts any object; what sets it apart is comparison by identity, not the type of the value.
There is a difference: ValueKey compares with `==`, ObjectKey with `identical`.

questions.prompt: What is `updateShouldNotify` for in an InheritedWidget?
options: It forces the InheritedWidget to rebuild
It decides whether to rebuild the dependents
questions.explanation: When the InheritedWidget is replaced, Flutter calls `updateShouldNotify(old)`: if it returns true, the widgets that depend on it are rebuilt.
whyWrong: It doesn't force the InheritedWidget to rebuild: it's called once the widget has already been replaced, to decide whether to notify the dependents.
ChangeNotifier has its own mechanism with `notifyListeners`; `updateShouldNotify` is about the InheritedWidget's dependents.
An InheritedWidget has no RenderObject of its own: `updateShouldNotify` only decides whether to rebuild whatever depends on it.

questions.prompt: Why is `dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType` O(1)?
options: Every Element has a map of its ancestor InheritedElements
It walks the tree with an LRU cache
questions.explanation: Every Element inherits a type -> InheritedElement map from its parent, so the lookup doesn't need to walk up the tree.
whyWrong: No tree walk and no LRU cache: every Element inherits a type -> InheritedElement map from its parent.
GlobalKeys have nothing to do with it: the lookup uses the InheritedElement map inherited from the parent.
The widget tree isn't balanced, and even if it were the cost would be O(log n); the O(1) comes from the per-type map.

questions.prompt: Which tree is the cheapest to recreate on every build?
questions.explanation: Widgets are lightweight, immutable objects: recreating them is cheap. Elements and RenderObjects are reused precisely because they're expensive.
whyWrong: Elements are expensive to recreate because they carry the State and the lifecycle: Flutter goes out of its way to reuse them.
RenderObjects hold layout and paint information: recreating them is expensive, which is why they're updated in place.
The Layer tree is for compositing during the paint phase; it's not what you recreate on every `build`.

questions.prompt: In a list, where does the key go?
options: On the innermost child that holds the state
On the root of each item, among the siblings
questions.explanation: Keys are compared among siblings of the same parent. A key nested deeper doesn't help match the list's items.
whyWrong: Keys are only compared among siblings: on a nested child they don't help match the list's items.
A key on the ListView identifies the whole list, not the individual items that need to be reconciled.
A key on the MaterialApp has no effect on how a list's items are reconciled.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType` and `getInheritedWidgetOfExactType`?
options: The first registers a dependency, the second doesn't
questions.explanation: Only `dependOn...` subscribes the widget to changes and causes rebuilds. `get...` reads the value once, which is handy in callbacks.
whyWrong: `getInheritedWidgetOfExactType` isn't deprecated: it's the right way to read without creating a dependency.
Both search only among ancestors, never descendants.
They aren't aliases: only `dependOn...` subscribes the widget and causes a rebuild when the value changes.

topics.title: State Management
topics.summary: setState, ChangeNotifier, Provider, Riverpod, BLoC/Cubit, and when to use each

lesson.heading: Ephemeral state vs. app state
lesson.body:
The Flutter docs distinguish **ephemeral state** (the selected tab, an animation, the text in a field), which lives happily in a `StatefulWidget` with `setState`, from **app state** (the logged-in user, a shopping cart, preferences) that is shared across screens.

Not everything belongs in a global solution: reaching for BLoC to manage a local toggle is over-engineering. The signal that you need something more is **prop drilling**, or business logic tangled up with the UI.

lesson.heading: ChangeNotifier and ValueNotifier
lesson.body:
`ChangeNotifier` is an observable class: you modify the state and call `notifyListeners()`. `ValueNotifier<T>` notifies automatically when you assign a new `value` that differs from the previous one.

Watch out: mutating an inner object (e.g. `value.add(x)` on a list) does **not** notify, because the reference doesn't change. In the UI, you listen with `ListenableBuilder` or `ValueListenableBuilder`.

lesson.heading: Provider
lesson.body:
Provider is a wrapper around InheritedWidget that simplifies dependency injection and listening for changes. `context.watch<T>()` rebuilds the widget when T notifies, `context.read<T>()` reads without subscribing (for callbacks), and `context.select` rebuilds only when a specific part changes.

It's simple and recommended by the Flutter team as a starting point, but it depends on `BuildContext`, and some errors (a missing provider) only surface at runtime.

lesson.heading: Riverpod
lesson.body:
Riverpod (from the same author as Provider) declares providers as immutable global variables, **independent of BuildContext**, with errors caught at compile time. You read with `ref.watch` in build and `ref.read` in callbacks, and use `ref.listen` for side effects.

It offers `Notifier`/`AsyncNotifier` for logic, `AsyncValue` for loading/error/data, `autoDispose` and `family`, and easy overrides in tests via `ProviderScope` or `ProviderContainer`.

lesson.heading: BLoC and Cubit
lesson.body:
BLoC strictly separates UI and logic: the UI sends **events**, and the Bloc emits **states** as a Stream. **Cubit** is the simplified version: public methods that call `emit(newState)`, with no events.

`BlocBuilder` rebuilds the UI, `BlocListener` runs one-off side effects (navigation, SnackBar), and `BlocConsumer` does both. It's highly testable (`bloc_test`) and predictable, at the cost of more boilerplate.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Typical question: **"Which state management do you use, and why?"** There's no single right answer, so show your criteria. `setState` for local state; Provider or Riverpod for shared state in small and mid-sized apps; BLoC when you need event traceability, large teams, and strict rules.

Mention the cross-cutting concepts: immutable state, UI/logic separation, granular rebuilds (`select`, `Consumer`), side effects kept out of build, testability. Walk through a real case where you made the call and what you'd do differently.

questions.prompt: The selected tab on a single screen should be managed with:
questions.explanation: It's ephemeral state, local to one widget: `setState` is the simplest correct solution.
whyWrong: BLoC is never mandatory: for local ephemeral state it would add complexity with no benefit.
A global Provider would expose to the whole app state that only one widget cares about.
SharedPreferences is for persisting to disk, not for managing in-memory UI state.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `context.watch<T>()` and `context.read<T>()`?
options: read is for lists, watch is for single objects
watch is async, read is synchronous
watch rebuilds on changes, read doesn't
questions.explanation: `watch` registers the widget as a dependent; `read` returns the value without subscribing, which makes it the right fit for callbacks like onPressed.
whyWrong: The type of the value is irrelevant: the difference is whether the widget subscribes to changes.
Both are synchronous and return the value immediately; the only difference is whether a dependency is registered.
There's an important difference: `watch` rebuilds the widget on changes, `read` doesn't.

questions.prompt: When `Cart` calls `notifyListeners()` but `count` hasn't changed, the widget:
questions.explanation: `select` compares the selected value before and after, and rebuilds only if it changed. Cutting down rebuilds is exactly what it's for.
whyWrong: `select` compares the selected value before and after: if `count` is the same, the rebuild is skipped.
No exception: `notifyListeners` is business as usual, and `select` simply ignores the notification.
The widget isn't even rebuilt, so there's no way for it to lose its state.

questions.prompt: What's the main difference between Cubit and Bloc?
options: Cubit has methods that emit, Bloc receives events
Bloc only works on Flutter web
questions.explanation: Both expose a Stream of states. A Cubit is driven by method calls, a Bloc by events mapped with `on<Event>`.
whyWrong: A Cubit also exposes a Stream of states: what differs is only how you feed it.
Bloc is highly testable: with `bloc_test` you verify the states emitted in response to events.
Bloc is pure Dart and runs on every platform, not just the web.

questions.prompt: What does `notifyListeners()` do in a ChangeNotifier?
questions.explanation: It synchronously invokes the registered listeners; it's builders like `ListenableBuilder` or Provider that schedule the rebuilds.
whyWrong: It doesn't rebuild anything directly: it calls the listeners, and only subscribed widgets schedule a rebuild.
`notifyListeners` doesn't save anything: persistence has to be handled separately.
You close a notifier with `dispose()`; `notifyListeners` leaves it active.

questions.prompt: What's the key advantage of Riverpod over Provider?
questions.explanation: Riverpod providers are declared globally and read through `ref`, so there's no `ProviderNotFoundException` at runtime, and you can access them outside widgets too.
whyWrong: Riverpod still uses an InheritedWidget, `ProviderScope`, to expose the container: the advantage is not depending on the context to read.
Compile speed isn't a distinguishing advantage; independence from BuildContext and compile-time safety are.
Riverpod supports mutable state too, e.g. with ChangeNotifierProvider; immutability is recommended, not enforced.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the UI update when `add` is called?
options: The list is mutated without reassigning `value`
questions.explanation: ValueNotifier only notifies in the `value` setter, when the new value is different. You need `value = [...value, x]`.
whyWrong: ValueNotifier accepts any type; the point is that it only notifies in the `value` setter, which isn't called here.
`dispose` releases resources but has nothing to do with notifications: even with dispose the UI wouldn't update.
Making `add` async wouldn't change anything: the list would still be mutated without going through the `value` setter.

questions.prompt: Where do you navigate or show a SnackBar in response to a Bloc state?
questions.explanation: The builder can run many times and must be pure; `BlocListener` is called once per state change, which makes it ideal for side effects.
whyWrong: The builder can run several times for the same state: navigating there would cause multiple pushes.
The Bloc's constructor has no BuildContext, and business logic shouldn't be dealing with navigation.
A Timer in `initState` is a hack: it doesn't react to state changes and risks using a context that's no longer valid.

questions.prompt: In Riverpod, inside `build()` you should use:
questions.explanation: `ref.watch` in build keeps the UI in sync; `ref.read` in callbacks avoids unnecessary rebuilds; `ref.listen` is for side effects.
whyWrong: With `ref.read` in build, the UI doesn't update when the provider changes: it reads the value just once.
`ref.listen` is for side effects like navigation or a SnackBar, and it doesn't return the value to display.
`context.watch` belongs to Provider; in Riverpod you read through `ref`.

questions.prompt: How do you justify your state management choice in an interview?
options: Scale, team, and testability; setState for local state
GetX, because it has less boilerplate
questions.explanation: No library is mandatory and Provider isn't deprecated: interviewers are looking for reasoned criteria, not an absolute preference.
whyWrong: Provider isn't deprecated and is still recommended; always picking the same library shows no judgment.
Boilerplate isn't the only criterion: GetX is often criticized for tight coupling and poor testability.
There's no single standard: BLoC is a good fit for large apps, but always imposing it ignores scale and context.

topics.title: Navigation
topics.summary: Navigator 1.0, named routes, Router, go_router, results, and deep links

lesson.heading: Navigator 1.0
lesson.body:
The `Navigator` manages a **stack of routes** imperatively: `push` adds a screen, `pop` removes it. `pushReplacement` replaces the current route (e.g. splash to home), and `pushAndRemoveUntil` clears the stack down to a condition (e.g. after login or logout).

`MaterialPageRoute` and `CupertinoPageRoute` provide platform transitions, including swipe-back on iOS.

lesson.heading: Passing data and results
lesson.body:
You pass data to the new screen through its **constructor**. To get a result back, `push` returns a `Future<T?>` that completes when the route is closed with `pop(context, value)`.

The result is **nullable**: if the user goes back with the gesture or the system button, the Future completes with `null`. After the `await`, check `context.mounted` before using the context.

lesson.heading: Named routes
lesson.body:
With `routes` or `onGenerateRoute` on `MaterialApp`, you navigate with `pushNamed('/details', arguments: id)` and read the arguments with `ModalRoute.of(context)!.settings.arguments`.

The Flutter docs now **recommend against** named routes for most apps: deep link behavior can't be customized, and on the web they don't handle the browser's forward button. The arguments are also `Object?`, so they aren't type-safe.

lesson.heading: Navigator 2.0 and Router
lesson.body:
Navigator 2.0 (the Router API) is **declarative**: the page stack is derived from app state through a list of `Page` objects. A `RouterDelegate` builds the Navigator, and a `RouteInformationParser` converts URLs to state and back.

It was created to support web URLs, deep links, and arbitrary stack changes, but it's verbose. That's why in practice you use a package like **go_router**, maintained by the Flutter team.

lesson.heading: go_router and deep links
lesson.body:
go_router maps URLs to screens with `GoRoute(path: '/users/:id')` and reads parameters from `state.pathParameters` and `state.uri.queryParameters`. `context.go` **sets the stack** based on the URL, while `context.push` adds a route on top of the current stack.

`redirect` centralizes guards (e.g. authentication), and `ShellRoute` and `StatefulShellRoute` handle persistent layouts and bottom navigation with one stack per tab. Deep links also need native configuration: App Links on Android, Universal Links on iOS (Associated Domains + an `apple-app-site-association` file).

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Typical question: **"How do you handle navigation, auth, and deep links in a Flutter app?"** A concise answer: go_router with declarative, URL-based routing, `redirect` for the auth guard (with `refreshListenable` to react to login), `StatefulShellRoute` for tabs, and native configuration for App Links and Universal Links.

If they ask about Navigator 1.0 vs. 2.0: the first is imperative and simple, while the second makes the stack a function of state, which you need for the web and complex deep links.

questions.prompt: How do you get a value back from a screen that's being closed?
options: With setState in the child screen
questions.explanation: `push` returns a Future that completes with the value passed to `pop`. It's the idiomatic way to get results.
whyWrong: A global variable creates coupling and hard-to-trace bugs: `push` already returns a Future with the result.
`setState` only updates the child screen's State and passes nothing back to the previous screen.
`Navigator.replace` swaps out a route and doesn't return any result.

questions.prompt: After login, "back" must not return to the login screen. What do you use?
questions.explanation: Replacing the route (or clearing the stack) removes login from the history; with `push` it would stay underneath home.
whyWrong: With `push`, login stays in the stack under home: pressing back would take you there.
`maybePop` closes the current route if it can, but doesn't remove login from the history.
`popUntil` removes routes from the top, but doesn't put home in place of login.

questions.prompt: The user closes the page with the system back button. What does this print?
questions.explanation: Closing without passing a value to `pop` completes the Future with `null`: that's why the result type is `bool?`.
whyWrong: Closing without a value doesn't produce `false`: the Future completes with `null`, which is why the type is `bool?`.
`true` only comes back if the page calls `pop(context, true)`; the system back button passes no value.
Closing with back isn't an error: the Future completes normally, just with `null`.

questions.prompt: In go_router, what's the difference between `context.go` and `context.push`?
options: go sets the stack from the URL, push adds on top
push only works on the web
questions.explanation: `go` navigates to a location, rebuilding the stack according to the route hierarchy; `push` stacks a new page and lets you go back.
whyWrong: There's an important difference: `go` rebuilds the stack from the location, `push` adds a page on top.
`push` works on every platform; on the web, at most the way the URL gets updated changes.
It's the other way around: `go` returns nothing, while `push` returns a Future with the pop result.

questions.prompt: With `GoRoute(path: '/users/:id')`, how do you read `42` from `/users/42`?
questions.explanation: `:param` segments end up in `pathParameters`; query parameters (`?id=42`) are in `uri.queryParameters`; `extra` is an arbitrary object that isn't in the URL.
whyWrong: `extra` is an arbitrary object passed during navigation, not extracted from the URL: it doesn't contain `42`.
`queryParameters` reads the part after `?`, like `?id=42`; `:id` is a path segment.
`ModalRoute.settings` belongs to the classic Navigator; go_router exposes the segments in `state.pathParameters`.

questions.prompt: Why was Navigator 2.0 (the Router API) introduced?
options: Declarative stack: web URLs and deep links
questions.explanation: The imperative API couldn't rebuild the stack from state or from a URL. Router makes the stack a function of app state.
whyWrong: Hero animations already worked with Navigator 1.0; the reason was declarative stack management.
MaterialPageRoute is used with the Router API too; the goal wasn't to replace routes.
Navigator 1.0 has always supported `pop`; what was missing was the ability to rebuild the stack from state or a URL.

questions.prompt: Where do you implement "if not authenticated, go to /login" with go_router?
questions.explanation: `redirect` is evaluated on every navigation and can return an alternative location; with `refreshListenable` it also reacts to login changes.
whyWrong: Checking in every `build` duplicates the logic and briefly shows the protected page; `redirect` centralizes it.
In `main`, the check runs only once and doesn't react to later logouts or deep links.
`onGenerateRoute` belongs to the classic Navigator; with go_router the right place is the `redirect` callback.

questions.prompt: Bottom navigation where each tab keeps its own stack:
options: StatefulShellRoute or one Navigator per tab
questions.explanation: You need a nested Navigator per tab; go_router's `StatefulShellRoute` does this and preserves the state of each branch.
whyWrong: With a single Navigator and `pushReplacement` you lose the history: every tab switch throws away the previous stack.
IndexedStack preserves widget state, but without nested Navigators it has no per-tab stack.
Named routes use a single Navigator: arguments don't create separate stacks for the tabs.

questions.prompt: According to the Flutter docs, what's the main limitation of named routes (`pushNamed`)?
options: Limited deep link customization, no forward on the web
questions.explanation: The docs recommend against them for most apps because of these limitations; arguments exist, but they're untyped `Object?`.
whyWrong: Named routes accept arguments via `arguments`; the limitation is that they're untyped `Object?`.
They weren't removed: they still exist, but the docs recommend against them for most apps.
They work on every platform, iOS included; the limitations concern deep links and the web.

questions.prompt: What do you need on iOS to open the app from an https link (Universal Links)?
options: Nothing, it works out of the box
questions.explanation: iOS verifies the domain through the Associated Domains entitlement and the AASA file on the server; Flutter then passes the path to the router.
whyWrong: You don't need a custom MethodChannel: Flutter already receives the link and passes it to the router.
AndroidManifest configures Android App Links; on iOS you need Associated Domains and the AASA file.
iOS has to verify that the domain belongs to your app: without the entitlement and AASA, the link opens in Safari.

topics.title: Isolates and Concurrency
topics.summary: The isolate model, SendPort and ReceivePort, compute, background work, and the limits of unshared memory

lesson.heading: The isolate model
lesson.body:
Dart doesn't have threads that share memory: it has **isolates**. Each isolate has its own heap, its own event loop, and its own garbage collector, and it can't touch another isolate's memory. The only way for them to talk is to **pass messages**.

That leads to the point worth making first in an interview: since nothing shares memory, Dart **has no locks, mutexes, or data races**. The trade-off is that you can't mutate an object "from another thread" either: you have to send it.

A Flutter app starts on a single isolate, the **main isolate**, which is the one that builds the widgets. `async`/`await` doesn't leave it: that's concurrency on the same event loop, not parallelism. A loop that hogs the CPU for 300 ms blocks frames even if the function is `async`.

lesson.heading: SendPort and ReceivePort
lesson.body:
`Isolate.spawn` starts a new isolate from an entry-point function, which must be **top-level or static** (not a closure that captures variables: the new isolate doesn't have that state), and passes it **a single initial message**.

Channels come in pairs: the **ReceivePort** is the listening end, and its `sendPort` is the writing end. Whoever opens the port keeps the ReceivePort and hands out the SendPort. To get a reply, the parent sends its own SendPort inside the initial message: that's the *handshake* you see in almost all isolate code.

As long as a ReceivePort stays open, the isolate stays alive: close it with `close()`, or it will sit there eating memory.

lesson.heading: compute and Isolate.run
lesson.body:
For a single heavy job you don't need the whole handshake: `compute(fn, arg)` (from `package:flutter/foundation.dart`) spins up a throwaway isolate, runs the function, and returns the result. Since Dart 2.19 there's the pure-Dart equivalent `Isolate.run`, which also accepts a closure.

They're the right choice for **CPU-bound** work: parsing a large JSON payload, decoding or resizing images, cryptography, sorting huge lists. They're not for **I/O**: an HTTP call or a file query is already asynchronous and doesn't block the isolate, so moving it to another isolate only adds cost.

Because `compute` has a cost too: spawning the isolate and **copying** the argument and result takes a few milliseconds. Below ~10 ms of work, it's often better to stay on the main isolate; if the work is continuous, keep a long-lived worker isolate instead of creating one per request.

lesson.heading: Background work
lesson.body:
"Background" means two different things in Flutter, and mixing them up is a classic interview mistake.

A secondary isolate runs **off the UI thread but inside the app's process**: when the OS suspends the app, the isolates stop with it. For work that has to keep going after the app is closed, you need the native APIs: `BGTaskScheduler`/background modes on iOS, `WorkManager` or a foreground service on Android, typically through `workmanager` or the FCM background handler.

A secondary isolate also **doesn't have the Flutter bindings**: platform channels are tied to the root isolate. If you need a plugin there, pass a `RootIsolateToken` and register the messenger with `BackgroundIsolateBinaryMessenger.ensureInitialized`.

lesson.heading: What can't cross between isolates
lesson.body:
`send` makes a **deep copy** of the message. The exceptions are immutable objects (`String`, numbers, `bool`, `null`, constants), which are passed by reference, and top-level or static functions, which can be sent as references.

You can't send: closures that capture mutable state, objects holding a native resource (sockets, database handles, FFI `Pointer`s), and of course nothing tied to the UI — `BuildContext`, widgets, `State`. If you try, you get a runtime error.

For large data, the copy is the main cost: `TransferableTypedData` **transfers** a block of bytes without copying it (the sender loses it), and `Isolate.exit(port, result)` returns the result while shutting down the isolate, again without a copy.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Typical question: **"Dart is single-threaded, so how do you do heavy work without blocking the UI?"** Answer: it depends. If it's I/O, I do nothing special: it's already asynchronous and the event loop stays free. If it's CPU-bound, I move it to another isolate with `compute` or `Isolate.run`, because `async` on its own moves nothing: it still runs on the same thread.
